name: Kessler Interchange
description: Where four of GLMZ's primary transit corridors converge in a massive multilevel interchange complex, Kessler has evolved from pure infrastructure into something closer to a city-state in miniature. The interchange handles magnetic rail, freight conveyance, autonomous vehicle routing, and pedestrian transit simultaneously across seventeen stacked levels, and the sheer density of passing traffic has generated a permanent commercial and residential layer that exists entirely within the interchange structure itself. Shops, clinics, hostels, and service providers have colonized every platform, mezzanine, and maintenance corridor not actively required for transit operations.

sights: seventeen levels of rail and walkway visible simultaneously in the central atrium
departure and arrival boards covering entire walls in cascading information
freight containers moving on automated tracks overhead
the constant flow of transit passengers mixing with permanent residents
vendor kiosks wedged into every structural recess
maintenance workers in hi-vis gear navigating through civilian crowds
sounds: rail tone warnings cycling constantly at different frequencies per level
the deep resonant vibration of heavy freight passing through
crowd noise amplified and distorted by the atrium's acoustics
automated routing announcements in synthesized voices
the squeal of rail brakes from every direction
smells: hot brake material and electrical discharge
food vendors from a dozen cultures cooking simultaneously
recycled air pushed through inadequate ventilation
atmosphere.feel: Relentless and disorienting — a space that was never designed for stillness, where everyone is always arriving, departing, or waiting, and where the permanent residents have learned to find stability in perpetual motion.

demographics: An extraordinarily diverse transient population supplemented by 8,000–12,000 permanent or semi-permanent residents. Transit workers make up the largest stable group, followed by service and retail workers serving the interchange economy. A significant refugee and asylum-seeking population uses Kessler as a staging point, exploiting the jurisdictional ambiguity of a transit hub that nominally belongs to the Meridian Transit Authority but is too large and complex to effectively police.
economy: Transit services and commercial retail at the primary level, supplemented by an enormous informal economy in transit documentation assistance, luggage and cargo handling, currency exchange, short-term accommodation, and the services that travelers need and don't want recorded. Kessler is one of the few places in Meridian where physical currency still circulates freely, because the transit authority's financial monitoring systems have never been successfully extended to the interchange's colonized commercial spaces.
power_structure: The Meridian Transit Authority holds nominal jurisdiction but exercises it selectively, focusing on the transit infrastructure itself and ignoring the colonized commercial and residential spaces provided those spaces don't disrupt operations. Real authority is distributed among level-specific merchant associations, the Transit Workers Union (which controls all actual infrastructure maintenance), and the Kessler Residents Collective, which formed to negotiate with the Transit Authority over eviction threats that resurface periodically.
dangers: getting lost in the maintenance level network, which extends far beyond official maps
transit authority sweeps that periodically clear informal residents with minimal notice
freight routing errors that send automated cargo through occupied spaces
pickpockets and short-con operators targeting transit passengers
the jurisdictional gaps that make violent crime difficult to report
corporate bounty hunters using the interchange's anonymity to locate targets
opportunities: access to transit routes connecting every major district in GLMZ
the physical cash economy operating outside corporate financial monitoring
forged or facilitated transit documentation for travel under false identity
cargo access — both legitimate and otherwise — to the freight network
a genuinely anonymous population where disappearing into the crowd is achievable
the Transit Workers Union as an organized body with access to every level of Meridian infrastructure
story_hooks: A freight container arrived on an automated route from a destination that doesn't exist in the routing system, and the Transit Authority is very quietly trying to retrieve it before anyone opens it
A child has been living alone in the maintenance levels for months, navigating them with a map that predates Meridian's construction
The Transit Workers Union is planning a total work stoppage — and someone has hired a crew to prevent it through means that aren't limited to negotiation
A series of passengers on inbound rail lines have arrived with no memory of boarding, all departing from different origin points

Level Nine has been informally closed for three weeks following an incident the Transit Authority won't describe, and the residents who lived there are scattered throughout the interchange with no explanation
frequented_by: refugees and people in transit between identities
bounty hunters and skip tracers using the hub to intercept targets

notable_locations.name: The Atrium Floor
notable_locations.description: The central open space at the interchange's mid-levels where all seventeen tiers are visible simultaneously. The nominal center of Kessler's informal civic life — the location of the only public screens in the interchange, the largest vendor concentration, and the unofficial meeting ground where the Residents Collective holds open assemblies.

notable_locations.name: Sub-Level Maintenance Grid
notable_locations.description: The labyrinthine infrastructure layer beneath the transit decks, officially accessible only to Transit Workers Union members. In practice, a parallel city of informal spaces, hidden rooms, and passageways that experienced residents use to navigate the interchange without entering the monitored transit areas. Contains several long-term habitations that have existed for over a decade.

notable_locations.name: The Paper District
notable_locations.description: An informal name for the cluster of Level Four kiosks and back-room operators who provide documentation services — transit passes, identity verification, cargo manifests, and travel records — in degrees of legitimacy ranging from fully authorized to entirely fabricated. The Transit Authority knows it exists and has calculated that disrupting it would cause more operational problems than tolerating it.
